China’s industrial profit growth is losing momentum:

China’s industrial profits rose +4.2% YoY in August, the weakest YoY growth since November 2025.

This also marks the 4th consecutive monthly slowdown in growth.

Pressure is particularly visible in consumer-facing industries, where profits are falling in autos, clothing, and furniture.

Domestic demand continues to weaken, with consumption growth slowing to near zero while manufacturers, property developers, and infrastructure builders are cutting spending.

For the first 8 months of 2026, industrial profits were still up +15.7% YoY, but the gains are becoming increasingly concentrated, with the electronics industry contributing ~66% of total growth.

At the same time, raw-material industries contributed +6.2 percentage points to the overall increase, supported by higher commodity prices.

Weak domestic demand is weighing on China’s economy.

Lance Roberts
posts.text:
Fair context, Luke, and I agree the starting point is worse. Full-employment deficits near 6% of GDP, NIIP near -90%, and a larger offshore dollar short all raise the term premium and the risk of fiscal-credibility shocks. No argument there.

But I'd push back on "every crisis since." The 10-yr bottomed in Aug 2020, after the recession ended in April, and rose on recovery and 9% inflation. In the SVB crisis yields fell sharply. In the Aug 2024 yen carry unwind they fell again. April 2025 is the real counterexample, and I'd grant that one. But it was a basis-trade unwind over days, not a recession.

On NIIP, a large share of the deterioration is valuation. Foreigners own far more US equities, and US stocks have outperformed. Equity liabilities aren't a funding need the way debt is.

And a bigger offshore dollar short means a sharper dollar squeeze in a crisis, which means foreigners buying dollars. That's what the swap lines are built for.

So I'd frame it this way. These factors make yields more vulnerable during expansions and inflation scares. They haven't yet overridden the collapse in private demand that drives yields down in an actual recession.

The US deficit is surging despite low unemployment.

The cumulative US fiscal deficit since 2020 has surged to a massive $14.18 trillion.

Meanwhile, the 7-year average unemployment rate has fallen -0.4 percentage points, to 4.7% over the same period.

In the first 11 months of FY2026 alone, the US deficit totaled $1.97 trillion, the 3rd-largest for this period of the year in history.

When the economy is strong and unemployment is low, the government would typically keep fiscal deficits lower, reserving large-scale fiscal support for periods of economic weakness.

This time, however, the deficit is running at historically high levels despite stable unemployment.

This comes as elevated government spending and rising interest costs are keeping the deficit exceptionally large even without a recession.

Massive deficits have become a permanent feature of the US economy.

posts.name: Lance Roberts
posts.text:
On 1991: the deficit went from ~2.7% of GDP in FY89 to ~4.5% in FY92, closer to 200 bps than 600, and that included S&L resolution costs. More importantly, 1990 is the closest thing we have to austerity into a recession. The 1990 budget deal raised taxes and capped spending as the economy rolled over. The 10-yr fell from near 9% in 1990 to under 7% by late 1992.

On 2001: the swing from a 2.3% surplus to a ~3.4% deficit included two rounds of tax cuts and war spending. Even so, the 10-yr fell from ~6.5% in early 2000 to ~3.1% by mid-2003.

That's the pattern in every episode you cite. Deficits widened and yields fell. The market treated the added supply as safe-haven collateral, not a funding crisis.

On stimulus preventing a UST collapse, the sequence doesn't fit. The 10-yr hit ~2% in Dec 2008, two months before ARRA passed. In 2020 it hit ~0.5% weeks before CARES. Investors were buying Treasuries aggressively before stimulus arrived. The systemic risk sat in private credit and bank funding, and Treasuries were the refuge from it.

Growth above rates matters, agreed. But in recessions r falls along with g, because the Fed cuts and safe-haven demand rises. That's the deflationary dynamic I think the austerity math misses.

Here's what I found, and thanks again for the correction:

"It's almost always credited to Charles Darwin, but he never wrote or said it. The line comes from Leon C. Megginson, a professor of management and marketing at Louisiana State University, who was paraphrasing Darwin.

The original 1963 wording
Megginson's version appeared in "Lessons from Europe for American Business," published in the Southwestern Social Science Quarterly in 1963 (vol. 44, no. 1, p. 4):

"According to Darwin's Origin of Species, it is not the most intellectual of the species that survives; it is not the strongest that survives; but the species that survives is the one that is able best to adapt and adjust to the changing environment in which it finds itself."

He made a similar statement again in 1964 in Petroleum Management."

posts.name: Steve Burns
posts.text:
Trading is hard here are 10 rules that make it easier:

1. Only trade setups you understand.

2. Know your exit before your entry.

3. Position size small enough to think clearly.

4. Never turn a short-term trade into a long-term investment.

5. Don’t chase trends that are already over extended.

6. Let a price signal confirm your entry.

7. Take the loss when the setup fails and the stop loss is triggered.

8. Stay out when your edge isn’t there.

9. Judge the quality of decisions, not individual trade outcomes.

10. Quantify all your trading rules before your emotions and ego get engaged.
